# Introduction to Amos

## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of Amos

1. Amos introduced (1:1)
2. Yahweh judges the surrounding nations (1:2–2:3), the southern kingdom of Israel ((2:4–5) and the northern kingdom (2:6–16)
3. Yahweh condemns Israel’s injustice and religious hypocrisy (3–6)
4. Yahweh warns of coming judgment through visions (7:1–9:10)
5. Yahweh promises restoration and renewal for his people (9:11–15)

### What is the Book of Amos about?

The Book of Amos contains the words of Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa. Amos began to prophesy about 760 BC. He spoke Yahweh’s messages against God’s people behaving wickedly. He spoke messages to both the southern kingdom of Judah and the northern kingdom of Israel.

Yahweh gave Amos prophecies of judgment (Chapters 1–6) to proclaim to the people.

Three visions of Yahweh coming to judge the people are in the last part of the book (7:1–9:10). A final vision promises that Yahweh will restore Israel (9:11–15). He will restore the “tent of David.” This means a descendant of David would once again be king over Israel.

### How should the title of this book be translated?

The traditional title of this book is “The Book of Amos” or just “Amos.” Translators may also call it the “The Book of the Sayings of Amos.”

### Who wrote the Book of Amos?

The prophet Amos probably wrote this book. He lived in the southern kingdom of Judah. Amos came from a poor family. They grew sycamore trees (7:14-15) and were shepherds (1:1). Though Amos was not trained as a prophet, he knew and understood the law of Moses.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### How is justice described in Amos?

Justice is an important theme in the Book of Amos. Justice means people treating others fairly according to the law of Yahweh. People in Israel were oppressing and taking advantage of poor people, orphans, and widows. Amos explained that Yahweh would prefer that the people act justly rather than sacrifice to him. Truly obeying the law of Moses meant being just to other people.

### What is a lawsuit?

Many cultures have a process for resolving disputes through the use of courts. These legal disputes are called lawsuits. Amos uses various legal terms. Part of the book presents events in a courtroom. The people are introduced, the problem is explained, the people are examined, witnesses speak, and a verdict is given.

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### What is the meaning of the term “Israel”?

The name “Israel” is used in many different ways in the Bible. Jacob was a son of Isaac. God changed Jacob’s name to Israel. The descendants of Jacob became a nation also called Israel. Eventually, the nation of Israel split into two kingdoms. The northern kingdom was named Israel. The southern kingdom was named Judah. In Amos, “Israel” almost always refers to the northern kingdom of Israel.

### Where do the various narratives begin and end?

The structure of the Book of Amos may make it difficult to understand where Amos ends one thought and begins another. It may be helpful to solve these issues with carefully divided lines or paragraphs.

This traditional Hebrew poetic device continues as in chapter 1 which means complete or overflowing guilt.

# Amos 3 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh holds Israel accountable for rejecting him.

1. Yahweh declares Israel accountable because he chose them (1–2)
2. Yahweh warns of coming judgment and calls his people to listen (3–10)
3. Yahweh announces the destruction of Israel’s wealth and false security (11–15)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The horns of the altar

These projections at the corners of an altar were grasped for refuge; cutting them off (verse 14) means there is no refuge.

### Rhetorical questions

The prophet Amos uses a chain of rhetorical questions to illustrate that God’s judgment on Israel is the expected outcome. Just as everyday causes naturally produce predictable effects, Israel’s persistent sin makes divine disaster an absolute certainty.

Amos is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were the **sons** of their ancestor Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [against you Israelites]

Here, **all of the family** represents all of the descendants of those who were captive in Egypt. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of you descendants of those]

Amos first refers to **Yahweh** and then he uses the first person **I** to describe what Yahweh had done. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the second person throughout this verse as in the UST.

The implication is that when Yahweh says that he has **known** Israel, he means that he chose this people to belong to him in a special covenant relationship. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Only you have I chosen to be in a covenant relationship with me]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the nations or people groups that live on the earth. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the people groups that live on the earth]

Yahweh is using **I will visit upon you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will punish you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will punish you for]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [everything you have done wrong]

Yahweh, through Amos, is using the question form to emphasize the certainty of the fact that two people do not travel together unless they have arranged to do so. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Certainly two will not walk together, unless they have agreed!]
The pronoun **they** refers to the two people who agreed to walk together. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [unless the two of them have agreed]

If your readers would not be familiar with what a shofar is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Here and in the next verse, it could be that: (1) Amos is speaking about Yahweh as modeled in the UST (end Yahweh’s quote at the end of [verse 2](../..03/02.md)) or (2) Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person throughout these verses. Alternate translation: [I, the Lord Yahweh]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the secret plans that he himself has made. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Yahweh is speaking of the message he’s giving to the people through Amos as if it were the roar of a **lion** that everyone who hears it must fear (see [1:2](../01/02.md). Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has roared like a lion]

If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize the fact that when Lord Yahweh has spoken to his prophet, that prophet must proclaim his message. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. The implication is that the messengers are to make this proclamation to the people who live in **the citadels in Ashdod** and in **the citadels in the land of Egypt.** You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Proclaim to the people]

Here, **on the citadels** represents the rulers and other powerful people who live in those citadels. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Tell those who are Ashdod’s rulers and who rule]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and tell them to gather]

The expression **Be gathered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Gather yourselves]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **uproars**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how greatly the people in her midst are rioting]
The pronoun **her** refers to the city of Samaria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in Samaria]

Yahweh is using the adjective **oppressed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and the oppressed people within her]
The pronoun **they** refers to the people who live in Samaria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the inhabitants of Samaria do not know to do right]

Amos is using **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Here, **violence and destruction** represents the wealth that was attained and stored up as a result of the nation’s acting violently and destructively toward others. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [wealth gained through violence and destruction]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **violence** and **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what they have violently and destructively seized]

The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Because they have done these things]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [An adversary will come, and he will be all around the land]

The implication is that **An adversary** is an enemy army that will surround the land and attack its cities. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The army of the adversary will besiege the land on every side]

The pronoun **he** refers to the adversary, and the pronoun **you** refers to the land of Israel around Samaria and the people who live there. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And that adversary will bring down from you Israelites your strength]

Here, **your strength** represents the fortifications that the people of Israel trusted to protect them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And he will bring down your strong defenses]

If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as the shepherd can recover only parts of a sheep from the mouth of the lion, so only a small remnant of the sons of Israel will be rescued]

The expression **be rescued** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [thus I will only be able to rescue a few of the sons of Israel]

Here, **sons** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Jacob** means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [against the people descended from Jacob]

Amos is interjecting the phrase **the declaration of Yahweh** into what Yahweh is saying to emphasize that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the God who commands the armies of angels. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God, the commander of the angel armies]
Yahweh is using the term **in the day** to refer to at a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when the time comes for]

Yahweh is using **my visiting the transgressions of Israel upon him** as a common expression of the culture to mean “my punishing the people of Israel for their transgressions.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my punishing Israel for their transgressions]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgressions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the wrong things that Israel did]
The pronoun **him** refers to the nation of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [upon that nation]

Yahweh is using **I will also visit upon** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to come against” or “punish.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will also come against]

Here, **the horns of the altar** represents the protection that people superstitiously sought when they took hold of those horns. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the horns of the altar that people grasped for safety will be cut off]

Yahweh is the one who would do this. Alternate translation: [and I will cut off the horns of the altar]

The top corners of the central altar at Bethel (and others) were shaped like bull horns. These horns were a symbol of the strength of the god that was worshiped there. Yahweh is referring to all of the houses of the wealthy people of Israel by naming two extremes, **the winter house** and **the summer house**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of their many houses]

# Amos 4 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh calls Israel to repentance.

1. Yahweh condemns Israel’s oppression and indulgence (1–3)
2. Israel refuses to return to Yahweh despite his warnings (4–11)
3. Yahweh warns Israel to prepare to meet him (12–13)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Returning to Yahweh

Each disaster in verses 6–11 closes with the refrain “yet you did not return as far as me.” To “return” is to repent and come back to Yahweh.

Amos is speaking to the wealthy women of Samaria, whom he calls **cows of Bashan**, although he knows that they cannot hear him. He is doing this to show his listeners in a strong way how he feels about the way these women oppress the poor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about these women. Alternate translation: [Hear this word about the cows of Bashan]

The word translated as **Listen** is an imperative, but it communicates a summons rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a summons. Alternate translation: [I call on you to hear this word]

Amos is speaking of the wealthy women of Samaria as if they were **cows of Bashan**, that is, well-fed cattle grazing in rich pasture. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you well-fed, pampered women]

The implication is that the **masters** of these women are their husbands. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the ones saying to their husbands]
If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [That they should bring something so they may drink]

The women are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Bring drinks to us]

Following the custom of the culture, the Lord Yahweh is swearing an oath by guaranteeing it by something sacred, his own **holiness**. Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. Alternate translation: [has solemnly promised, as surely as he is holy,]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by his holy name]

The word translated as **that** introduces the content of the oath that the Lord Yahweh has sworn. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [saying, behold]

Amos is putting the phrase **the breaches** before the verb in order to emphasize where the women will go out. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about their going out before the information about the place where they will go out. Alternate translation: [And you will go out, {through} the breaches]

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [each woman going out through the breach that is in front of her]

The pronoun **her** refers to the woman just ahead of each woman as they file out through the breaches. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [following the one ahead of her]

Amos is using this possessive form to mean the declaration that Yahweh is making. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [this is what Yahweh declares]

# Amos 5 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues to be written in a poetic format and foretells the destruction of the kingdom of Israel.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Place Names

This chapter refers to various places in land of Israel (i.e. Gilgal, Bethel, Beersheba). Normally these places have good connotations, but here they are referred to negatively. This is most likely because these cities became known for their idol worship. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-names]])

### City gate

The “city gate” is mentioned several times. This was a place where people would go with legal and financial issues. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues to be written in poetic style except for verses 9–10, which are in prose. These two verses contain many interested features.

The kingdoms of Judah (represented by Zion) and Israel (represented by Samaria) are being compared to the kingdoms represented by the cities named in this verse. Because of the parallel structure of the two questions in this verse, it is most likely that **they** refers to the cities that have just been named, and that **these kingdoms** refers to Judah and Israel. But since he refers to **your border**, it seems more likely that Amos is speaking to the “designated ones” and pointing out that, although God has made their kingdoms great, he will also destroy them because they are not better in the way that they should be. ## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is written in poetic form and it shows the way Yahweh’s people are sinning and
 how he is going to respond. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/peopleofgod]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “This is the declaration of Yahweh”

This phrase is used to introduce prophecy. It highlights what God is proclaiming. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

Quote: Look, a basket of summer fruit!
Note: The word “look” here shows that Amos saw something interesting. Alternate translation: [I saw a basket of summer fruit!]
Alternate translation: [ripe fruit]
Yahweh uses a question to teach Amos. Alternate translation: [Tell me what you see, Amos.]

The word translated as **summer fruit** sounds very much like the word for **end**. Yahweh’s purpose in showing Amos summer fruit was to give him a prophecy of the end of his people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.
Alternate translation: [at that time]
This could mean: (1) Yahweh is to telling the people to be silent as they hear about the severity of his punishment or (2) the people will be silent because of their grief after Yahweh’s punishment.
Amos is speaking to the wealthy merchants who harm those who are poor.

Note: This can be restated to remove the nominal adjectives “the needy” and “the poor.” Alternate translation: [you who trample those who are in need and remove those in the land that are poor]
